items.correctExplanation: True — the classic result stands: your door keeps one-third while the survivor collects two-thirds.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. The host's forced reveal concentrates two-thirds onto the survivor; your door never improved.
items.lessonContent:
Forced reveals move probability onto survivors.
Your first pick freezes at one-third forever.
Rules behind reveals are worth real odds.

items.question: In the classic three-door game with a knowing host, switching wins two times in three.
items.title: The Two-Thirds Rule

items.correctExplanation: False — staying wins one-third, not one-half. Two doors left never implied equal odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Staying keeps the original one-third; the survivor holds two-thirds.
items.lessonContent:
Two survivors with unequal histories deceive counters.
'One of two' is not 'fifty-fifty' without equal pasts.
Histories weight doors; counts merely list them.
Share this: kill one fifty-fifty myth with a backstory.
items.question: After the classic reveal, staying with your first pick wins half the time.
items.title: The Loyal Half

items.correctExplanation: True — your door's 1% never grows while 99% piles onto the survivor. Scale exposes the machine.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. One pick in a hundred is almost surely wrong, and 98 reveals leave one heir to 99%.
items.lessonContent:
Scaling to a hundred doors silences intuition.
Tiny first-pick odds never grow through reveals.
Scale any puzzle until the answer screams.
Share this: convert one skeptic with the hundred-door tale.
items.question: With 100 doors and 98 goats revealed, the surviving door hides the car 99 times in 100.
items.title: The Ninety-Nine Percent

items.correctExplanation: False — a clueless random reveal carries zero information. Only knowing hosts move odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. The host stumbled blindly, so both closed doors stand truly equal.
items.lessonContent:
Ignorant reveals are accidents, not news.
Ask what the revealer knew before updating.
Knowledge moves odds; luck merely decorates.
Share this: separate one signal from one accident today.
items.question: If the host opens a random door without knowing anything and finds a goat, switching still doubles your odds.
items.title: The Lucky Stumble

items.correctExplanation: True — an early reveal informs everyone equally, which helps no one. Timing is everything.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. News before commitment spreads evenly across all doors, favoring none.
items.lessonContent:
Information must follow commitment to favor anyone.
Early news is public; late news is leverage.
Commit, then let information work.
Share this: notice one decision where order ruled.
items.question: A goat revealed before anyone picks leaves all doors at one-third each.
items.title: The Premature Curtain

items.correctExplanation: False — swapping blind trades one one-third for another. Motion without news is theater.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. No reveal means no information, so the swap changes nothing at all.
items.lessonContent:
Ceremony without information is pure theater.
Demand the reveal before paying motion's price.
Stillness beats motion in newsless games.
Share this: skip one purposeless swap and smile.
items.question: Offered a blind swap with no door opened, switching is smarter than staying.
items.title: The Blind Swap

items.correctExplanation: False — the survivor inherited the opened doors' share. Counts deceive; histories decide.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. One door carries its original third plus the revealed share; the other carries only its third.
items.lessonContent:
Equal counts never guarantee equal chances.
Audit histories before splitting odds evenly.
Fifty-fifty needs symmetric pasts, not pairs.
Share this: refuse one lazy fifty-fifty today.
items.question: Two closed doors remaining always means a fifty-fifty chance each.
items.title: The Lazy Half

items.correctExplanation: True — without shared history, no concentration happened for them. Odds are personal.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. They made no first pick, so no reveal ever worked in their favor.
items.lessonContent:
Probability belongs to observers with histories.
Latecomers inherit furniture, never fortunes.
Borrow numbers only with their backstories.
Share this: explain fresh odds to a late joiner.
items.question: A newcomer who saw nothing and picks between the two closed doors faces fifty-fifty.
items.title: The Fresh Eyes

items.correctExplanation: True — watching transfers the full informational situation. Attention, not participation, carries the edge.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. They witnessed pick plus forced reveal, so the two-thirds sits identically for them.
items.lessonContent:
Spectators with complete history bet like players.
Information rides attention across seats.
Watch fully before playing blindly.
Share this: learn one game by pure watching first.
items.question: A spectator who watched the pick and reveal inherits the switch edge.
items.title: The Keen Spectator

items.correctExplanation: True — openings conditioned on winning announce winning. Policy leaks through behavior.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. This host's rule turns every curtain into a winner's certificate.
items.lessonContent:
Conditioned actions confess their conditions.
Read policies, not moves, at strange tables.
'Why now' outranks 'what now'.
Share this: decode one policy hiding in one action.
items.question: A host who opens doors only for first-pick winners has, by opening, announced your win.
items.title: The Winner's Curtain

items.correctExplanation: True — openings conditioned on losing announce losing. Flee while flight is offered.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. The rule guarantees your door is wrong whenever curtains move.
items.lessonContent:
Reverse-conditioned reveals are warnings in costume.
Learn each table's grammar of curtains.
Meta-rules dominate visible moves.
Share this: memorize one house rule before playing.
items.question: Curtains at this carnival rise solely to expose losing first picks. One rises tonight. What does it expose?
items.title: The Mocking Curtain

items.correctExplanation: False — A stays at one-third; the freed third flows entirely to C. News about B spends B's share.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Naming B sacrifices B's slice to C alone; A's pardon chance never budged.
items.lessonContent:
Condemned men's shares flow to survivors, never to you.
Track whose slice news spends.
Thirds conserve across cells and doors.
Share this: retell the prisoners' twist correctly.
items.question: After the warden names B to die, prisoner A's pardon chance rises to one-half.
items.title: The Doomed Third

items.correctExplanation: True — gold drawers cluster in the double-gold box. Samples weight hypotheses by their yield.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Three gold drawers against three silver put double weight on the all-gold box.
items.lessonContent:
Draws sample contents, and rich boxes yield more.
Count drawers, never boxes, in box paradoxes.
Yield-weighting fixes container-counting errors.
Share this: demo Bertrand's boxes with pocket coins.
items.question: Drawing gold from a mixed trio of boxes means the same box hides gold again two-thirds of the time.
items.title: The Gilded Pair

items.correctExplanation: True — staying keeps one-fifth while four-fifths splits across two survivors. Either switch doubles fate.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Two reveals divide the 80% remainder evenly: 40% per survivor against 20% staying.
items.lessonContent:
Remainders divide among every survivor fairly.
Count survivors before crowning movers.
Partial sweeps still favor motion.
Share this: split one remainder across survivors by hand.
items.question: With five doors and two goats revealed, each surviving other door wins 40% of the time.
items.title: The Split Remainder

items.correctExplanation: True — the 75% remainder splits over two doors at 37.5% each, both beating 25% staying.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. One reveal among four doors leaves two heirs sharing three-quarters.
items.lessonContent:
Single reveals among many doors share their bounty.
Every survivor outranks the original pick here.
Small edges compound across repeated plays.
Share this: compute one four-door split aloud.
items.question: With four doors and one goat revealed, each other door beats staying 37.5% to 25%.
items.title: The Shared Bounty

items.correctExplanation: False — symmetry shields every door equally. Rituals pick lucky numbers; math picks none.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. No door outranks another pre-reveal, however selected.
items.lessonContent:
Symmetric choices deserve instant picks, not rituals.
Superstition taxes the hesitant with ceremony.
Spend deliberation on asymmetries only.
Share this: dice-decide one trivial pick today.
items.question: Always choosing door 1 outperforms choosing randomly each show.
items.title: The Ritual Door

items.correctExplanation: False — always-switch wins about two-thirds of simulated shows. Frequencies confirm fractions.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. A thousand simulated switchers collect roughly 667 wins, not 500.
items.lessonContent:
Simulations convert skeptics that proofs cannot.
Ten lines of code beat ten minutes of debate.
Frequency is theory made visible.
Share this: run one simulation for one doubter.
items.question: Simulating 1,000 always-switch shows yields about 500 wins.
items.title: The Simulated Thousand

items.correctExplanation: False — host policy writes the odds. Knowing, random, and rigged hosts play different games entirely.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Assumptions about the host ARE the calculation; change them and answers flip.
items.lessonContent:
Policies are parameters, never décor.
Audit the host before trusting textbook numbers.
Assumptions first, arithmetic second.
Share this: name one assumption behind one famous answer.
items.question: The host's knowledge and strategy are irrelevant to the correct odds.
items.title: The Irrelevant Host

items.correctExplanation: True — loaded priors stack with reveals: the example pushes switching to 80%. Evidence compounds with belief.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. A doubly-likely door plus a reveal elsewhere concentrates past the classic two-thirds.
items.lessonContent:
Priors and evidence stack instead of canceling.
Update twice: belief first, news second.
Loaded stages amplify textbook edges.
Share this: update one belief in two steps today.
items.question: Unequal prize placement can push the switching edge beyond two-thirds.
items.title: The Stacked Deck

items.correctExplanation: False — shuffling re-randomizes and destroys the information. Reset odds return to flat fifty-fifty.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Post-reveal shuffling erases history; the car sits randomly behind either door.
items.lessonContent:
Randomization burns information like fire burns paper.
Resets return every edge to zero.
Protect information from disturbance.
Share this: name one reset that erased an edge.
items.question: Re-shuffling the car randomly after the reveal preserves the switching edge.
items.title: The Erasing Shuffle

items.correctExplanation: True — two swaps net zero movement: the original one-third door returns. Ceremony can't launder odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. Switch-back equals never leaving; the one-third original greets you again.
items.lessonContent:
Round trips restore originals, never improve them.
Net movement is all arithmetic counts.
Motion masquerades as progress daily.
Share this: catch one return-trip posing as progress.
items.question: Switching to the survivor and then switching back leaves you at one-third.
items.title: The Round Trip

items.correctExplanation: False — rivals' doors hold their own thirds; no reveal moved anything. Company is decoration.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Without reveals, every contestant keeps an independent one-third regardless of crowds.
items.lessonContent:
Crowds dilute nothing without new information.
Independence ignores neighbors completely.
Envy of rival doors is innumeracy.
Share this: hold your pick calmly among crowds.
items.question: Other contestants picking different doors lowers your winning odds.
items.title: The Crowded Odds

items.correctExplanation: False — switching's expectation is about $6,667 against $4,000 certain. Arithmetic declines the bribe.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's false. Two-thirds of $10,000 outweighs $4,000 cash; take the odds, refuse the bribe.
items.lessonContent:
Price offers against expectation, never excitement.
Certainty seduces while arithmetic decides.
Shows monetize fear of variance.
Share this: compute one expectation before one offer.
items.question: A $4,000 walk-away bribe beats switching for a $10,000 car at two-thirds.
items.title: The Costly Bribe

items.correctExplanation: True — having picked the car, the host's rule forces a goat reveal. Constraint, not choice, opens the door.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. With the prize under your pick, every legal reveal shows a goat.
items.lessonContent:
Constraints masquerade as choices on game shows.
Forced moves carry information about the forcer.
Distinguish chosen reveals from compelled ones.
Share this: spot one forced move posing as free.
items.question: If you initially picked the car, the knowing host is forced to reveal a goat.
items.title: The Compelled Reveal

items.correctExplanation: True — conditioning on the pick is the whole engine. Unconditioned counting erases it and invents fifty-fifty.
items.incorrectExplanation: It's true. The reveal depends on your pick by rule; ignoring that dependence manufactures the fallacy.
items.lessonContent:
Dependence is the engine; independence the mirage.
Condition every probability on the rules that shaped it.
Fallacies are conditionings forgotten.
Share this: condition one everyday odd on its rules.
items.question: The fifty-fifty intuition fails because the reveal is conditioned on your first pick.
items.title: The Conditioned Reveal
